Profit and Loss Statement: Format, Example and Key Profit Lines

The profit and loss statement shows how much a company earned and spent over a period, and what was left. This guide walks through it line by line, using a worked example.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

A worked example

Sunrise Traders Ltd for the year ended 31 March (₹ lakh, with 10 lakh shares).

Line₹ lakhMargin
Revenue from operations1,000100%
Cost of goods sold(600)
Gross profit40040%
Operating expenses (salaries, rent, others)(150)
EBITDA25025%
Depreciation(50)
EBIT (operating profit)20020%
Interest(40)
Profit before tax (PBT)16016%
Tax at 25%(40)
Profit after tax (PAT)12012%

Earnings per share (EPS) = PAT ÷ shares = ₹120 lakh ÷ 10 lakh = ₹12.

What each profit line tells you

  • Gross profit: how much is left after direct costs. It reflects pricing power and input costs.
  • EBITDA: the cash earning power of operations, before financing and accounting charges such as depreciation.
  • EBIT: operating profit, after the cost of using fixed assets. It helps compare companies with different amounts of debt.
  • PBT: what is left after interest, showing the effect of debt.
  • PAT: the final profit belonging to shareholders, from which dividends may be paid and the rest added to reserves.

The accrual basis

Revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash has moved. A credit sale counts as revenue today though the cash comes later. That is why profit and cash differ, and why you should read the P&L together with the cash flow statement.

Format in India

Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 presents revenue from operations and other income, then expenses by nature (cost of materials, employee benefits, finance costs, depreciation and others), and then profit before and after tax. Companies also report consolidated figures that include subsidiaries.

How to read it well

  • Compare margins over 5 years and against peers, not just one year's profit.
  • Separate exceptional items, such as a one-off property sale, from recurring profit.
  • Check other income: profit that depends on it says little about the core business.
  • Compare profit with operating cash flow: profits that never turn into cash are a warning sign.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?

Gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of goods sold. Net profit is what remains after all expenses, interest and tax.

Is depreciation a cash expense?

No. The cash left when the asset was bought; depreciation spreads that cost over its useful life, and so it is added back in the cash flow statement.

What is the difference between a balance sheet and a P&L?

A balance sheet shows position on one date. A P&L shows performance over a period. Profit after dividends flows into reserves on the balance sheet, which links the two.
